To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the expression of genes involved in p53 signaling is altered in morphologically normal breast cells from TP53 mutation carriers, and this is likely to be important in the development of cancer.

the gene expression profiles of morphologically normal breast cells bearing a single TP53 mutation are altered and that these changes in gene expression parallel changes observed in the development of sporadic breast cancer.

we have identified a unique molecular signature of morphologically normal breast cells from TP53 mutation carriers and that this signature is likely to provide a basis for discovery of biomarkers and targets for chemoprervention of sporadic tumors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of gene expression signatures of normal cells that carry a "one-hit" in a tumor-suppressor gene.
the identification of molecular changes that occur early in the process of cancer development.
the development of molecular biomarkers that may be used to identify individuals at increased risk of developing cancer, and for early detection and chemoprevention.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the global gene expression profiles of morphologically normal breast tissue from LFS mutation carriers is significantly altered compared to that from non-LFS controls and that these changes are consistent with those previously reported for LFS-derived fibroblasts and LFS-associated breast cancer.

the global gene expression signature associated with TP53 loss of function in normal cells from Li-Faumeni syndrome patients is consistent with the known role of the p53 tumor suppressor in the control of cell proliferation, differentiation and apoptosis, and that these findings may have implications for chemopreventive strategies.
this work has provided the first global gene expression profile in morphologically normal breast cells bearing a single TP53 mutation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the molecular signatures of morphologically "normal" cells that carry a single inherited mutation in TP53, TP53 haplo-insufficiency, may provide clues to early changes in gene expression that occur in the process of carcinogenesis.

the molecular signature of TP53 haploisufficiency in morphologically normal LFS cells provides insight into the molecular basis of cancer initiation and suggests potential therapeutic approaches for prevention of sporadic tumors.

we have identified multiple changes in the gene expression profile of LFS cells, which may be useful for early detection of breast cancer in LFS mutation carriers, as well as for the discovery of novel targets for chemoprevetion of sporadic breast cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the molecular signatures of cells bearing one inherited hit in a tumor suppressive gene are remarkably similar to those of cells bearing multiple somatic hits.
a single mutation in TP53, even in the absence of other mutations, can lead to changes in gene expression and signaling pathways that may be relevant in the development of cancer.

the molecular signature of normal cells from Li-Franumeni syndrome mutation carries may provide a window into the early events of cancer development and may be useful in the discovery of novel biomarkers and targets for chemoprvention of sporadic cancers.
